passages.happening:
Jonathan says to the young man who carries his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the Philistine outpost on the other side.” He does not tell his father (verse 1). Saul is sitting under a pomegranate tree on the edge of Gibeah with about six hundred men, and with them is Ahijah the priest, wearing an ephod (verses 2-3).

Between Jonathan and the outpost is a pass with a cliff on each side, Bozez and Seneh (verses 4-5). Jonathan speaks to his armor-bearer: “Come, let us cross over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will work on our behalf. Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few” (verse 6). The young man answers, “Do all that is in your heart. Go ahead; I am with you heart and soul” (verse 7).

Jonathan sets a sign. They will show themselves. If the Philistines tell them to wait, they will stay where they are. If they say come up, they will go, because the LORD has given them into their hands (verses 8-10). The Philistines see them and call out, “Come on up, and we will teach you a lesson!” (verse 12).

Jonathan climbs on his hands and feet with his armor-bearer behind him, and the Philistines fall before him, about twenty men (verses 13-14). Terror strikes the whole Philistine camp. ‘Indeed, the earth quaked and panic spread from God’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 13 left Israel cornered: a huge Philistine army, six hundred men with Saul, and hardly a sword among them. This chapter sets two ways of leading side by side. Jonathan acts in bold faith, and God works through him. Saul sits under a tree.

The pass at Michmash lay in Benjamin, where a steep valley divides Geba on the south from Michmash on the north. Travelers and scholars have long identified the gorge with the modern Wadi Suweinit.

The priest with Saul is Ahijah, a great-grandson of Eli, whose house was condemned in chapter 2. The fallen priestly line is still serving beside the king who is beginning to fall.

Jonathan's words in verse 6 are the heart of the chapter. ‘Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.’ His faith is bold but not proud. He says perhaps. He asks for a sign. He trusts God's power, not any promise of his own success.

The word for saving is the root from which the names Joshua and, in its later Greek form, Jesus are built. In this chapter it describes rescue from an enemy, and the narrator will say plainly whose rescue it was.
passages.later: God had told Gideon that he had too many men, ‘lest Israel glorify themselves over Me’ (Judges 7:2), and a later king of Judah prayed in Jonathan's spirit: “O LORD, there is no one besides You to help the powerless against the mighty” (2 Chronicles 14:11).
passages.asks: Jonathan said, ‘Perhaps the LORD will work on our behalf.’ Ask what you would attempt if you believed that nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, by many or by few. And ask who has said to you, ‘I am with you heart and soul’, and to whom you could say it.

passages.t: The LORD saves Israel, and a foolish oath
passages.happening:
Saul's watchmen see the Philistine army melting away. Saul calls the roll and finds Jonathan and his armor-bearer missing (verses 16-17). He tells Ahijah to bring the ark of God, but as the noise in the Philistine camp grows, he says to the priest, “Withdraw your hand” (verses 18-19). Saul and his men march out and find the Philistines striking one another (verse 20). Hebrews who had been with the Philistines change sides, and Israelites hiding in the hills join the chase (verses 21-22). ‘So the LORD saved Israel that day’ (verse 23).

But Saul has put his men under an oath: “Cursed is the man who eats any food before evening, before I have taken vengeance on my enemies” (verse 24). In a forest there is honey on the ground, and no one dares to taste it (verses 25-26).

Jonathan had not heard the oath. He dips the end of his staff in the honeycomb and eats, ‘and his eyes brightened’ (verse 27). A soldier tells him of the oath. “My father has brought trouble to the land,” Jonathan replied (verse 29). If the troops had eaten, he says, the victory would have been greater (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
In verse 18 the traditional Hebrew text has Saul call for the ark of God. But the ark had been at Kiriath-jearim since chapter 7, and the Greek translation reads ephod. Many translators and scholars think the ephod is meant, since it was used to seek God's guidance. The ephod held the Urim and Thummim, sacred objects used to receive a yes or no from God. No one knows exactly what they looked like.

When Saul tells the priest to withdraw his hand, he breaks off the asking of God halfway, because events are moving too fast. He starts religious acts and does not finish them.

The Hebrews of verse 21 seem to be people connected with Israel but living under Philistine control. When the battle turns, they change sides.

Oaths were taken with deadly seriousness. A curse spoken in God's name was believed to bind the one who swore it and those placed under it. That is why the soldiers will not touch the honey.

Jonathan's verdict, that his father has brought trouble to the land, uses the verb that names the Valley of Achor, where Achan was judged for the trouble he brought on Israel. The reader is invited to ask who the real troubler of Israel is.
passages.later: The word for trouble recalls Joshua's words to Achan: “Why have you brought this trouble upon us?” (Joshua 7:25).
passages.asks: Saul's oath made his own soldiers too weak to finish the victory. Ask whether you have bound yourself or others with rules God never gave, and what they have cost. And ask who has paid for a promise you made too quickly.

passages.t: Meat with the blood, and a lot that falls on Jonathan
passages.happening:
By the end of the day the troops are faint. They rush on the plunder, slaughter animals on the ground, ‘and ate meat with the blood still in it’ (verse 32). Saul is told, and he has a large stone rolled in so that the animals can be slaughtered properly there (verses 33-34). ‘Then Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD’ (verse 35).

Saul wants to chase the Philistines all night, but the priest says, “We must consult God here” (verse 36). Saul asks God, ‘But God did not answer him that day’ (verse 37).

Saul decides that some sin has caused the silence, and swears that the guilty one will die, ‘even if it is my son Jonathan’ (verse 39). The people say nothing. By Urim and Thummim, and then by lot, Jonathan is picked out (verses 41-42). “I only tasted a little honey with the end of the staff that was in my hand. And now I must die?” (verse 43). Saul swears by God that Jonathan must die (verse 44).

The people refuse. They say that Jonathan won a great deliverance for Israel and that not a hair of his head will fall, ‘for with God’s help he has accomplished this today’ (verse 45). ‘So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die’ (verse 45). Saul gives up the chase, and the Philistines go home (verse 46).
passages.hearers:
The law forbade eating meat with the blood in it, because the life is in the blood. The blood was to be drained out and poured on the ground. Saul's hungry army, kept from food by his oath, breaks God's real law in its hurry. A leader's foolish rule has pushed his people into sin.

The large stone gave a proper place to slaughter. The note that this was Saul's first altar may be a quiet comment on how late he came to it.

The lot moves from the people, to Saul and Jonathan, to Jonathan alone, the way Achan was found in Joshua's day. In verse 41 the BSB follows the fuller Greek text, which names the Urim and Thummim. The shorter Hebrew is harder to read.

The people's word rescued normally means to ransom, to free by paying a price or giving a substitute. Some scholars think something was given in Jonathan's place. Others take it more generally as rescue. The text does not say how.

The chapter shows a king who keeps the letter of his own oath and tramples the heart of God's law, and who is ready to kill the son God had used to save Israel. The people see what Saul cannot: Jonathan acted with God's help.
passages.later: The law gives the reason for the rule the soldiers broke: ‘For the life of the flesh is in the blood’ (Leviticus 17:11), and ‘Only be sure not to eat the blood, because the blood is the life’ (Deuteronomy 12:23).
passages.hard:
Did God really answer through the lot and point to Jonathan, as if eating a little honey without knowing of the oath were a sin?

The chapter raises the question honestly. The lot did single out Jonathan, and God was silent to Saul. Readers take this in different ways. Some think the lot simply showed who had broken the oath, as a matter of fact, without God approving Saul's oath or its penalty. Jonathan was guilty under a rash vow he had never heard. Others stress that God's silence came first, and that it was a judgment on Saul's whole conduct: the asking of God broken off, the foolish oath, the troops driven to sin. On that reading the lot exposes Saul's folly more than Jonathan's fault.

On either reading the narrator clearly sides with Jonathan and the people. Jonathan acted with God's help, and the oath that would have killed him is shown to be Saul's error, not God's will.
passages.asks: The people would not let Saul kill the son God had used. Ask whether there is a rule you have kept so strictly that it has harmed someone God was using. And ask whether you would speak up, as the people did, when a leader's oath is about to do harm.

passages.happening:
After Saul becomes king, he fights his enemies on every side: Moab, Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah and the Philistines, and wherever he turns he wins (verse 47). ‘He fought valiantly and defeated the Amalekites, delivering Israel from the hands of its plunderers’ (verse 48).

His sons are Jonathan, Ishvi and Malchishua, and his daughters are Merab, the elder, and Michal, the younger (verse 49). His wife is Ahinoam, and the commander of his army is Abner, his cousin (verse 50).

“And the war with the Philistines was fierce for all the days of Saul. So whenever he noticed any strong or brave man, Saul would enlist him” (verse 52).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends with a summary of wars and family, a common way for the historian to close the main account of a king. It gives Saul real credit. He fought on every side and won, and he defeated the Amalekites. Before chapter 15 tells of his final rejection, the narrator is fair to him.

Two names here will matter soon. Michal, his younger daughter, will marry David. Abner, his commander, will be at his side to the end and beyond it.

The last verse looks ahead. The Philistine war will last all Saul's life, and it will end with his death on Mount Gilboa. And whenever Saul saw a strong or brave man, he took him into his service. The next brave young man he notices will be David.
passages.later: A later list in Chronicles names four of Saul's sons: ‘Saul was the father of Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal’ (1 Chronicles 8:33). After Saul's death Abner will make one of them king over the north (2 Samuel 2:8).
passages.asks: Saul won battles on every side and still lost his way. Ask whether success in your work has hidden a failure in your obedience. And ask whom you notice and gather around you, and why.
